A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Double Unprojected Textures (DUT). Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained and added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original rendering comparisons, geometry and appearance ablations, runtime measurements, and motion-capture and out-of-distribution evaluations in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds qualitative experiments on motion errors, loose clothing and long hair, novel lighting, and clothing removal.

M1.justification: Appendix K adds an environment-specific adaptation procedure: fine-tuning the trained model on sparse views under new illumination before feed-forward rendering. The core GeoNet/GauNet architecture, double unprojection, Gaussian scale refinement and losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The original DynaCap, ASH, THUman4.0 and OOD-motion coverage is retained. Appendices I–M substantially broaden tested conditions through injected pose errors, a subject with a loose dress and long hair, a new lighting environment, and topology changes during clothing removal.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains ENeRF, DVA, HoloChar and GHG; the geometry ablations retain DDC and LBS; and the OOD comparison retains HoloChar. No comparison method is added or removed from these experiments, and the new qualitative studies introduce no additional baseline method.

E3.justification: New protocols include manually perturbing the left elbow from 0° to 60°13′ and fine-tuning for new lighting using input views and frames excluded from testing (Appendices I and K). Existing benchmark splits, metrics, training schedules and runtime measurement procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 12–16 add substantial diagnostic coverage: sensitivity to increasing motion errors, challenging clothing and hair, lighting adaptation, a matched-pose illustration of deformation information in texture distortions, and a topology-change failure case. The earlier component ablations and sparse-versus-dense mocap analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average runtime over 100 frames with three repetitions and report OOD PSNR standard deviations of 1.41 for DUT and 1.89 for HoloChar. The new studies introduce no additional repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval or significance reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores, ablation scores and runtime measurements are retained. New qualitative findings substantially extend the results: reported good renderings through 7°46′ elbow error, recovery of dress and hair dynamics, rendering after lighting adaptation, and degraded quality during clothing removal. These concern added conditions rather than performance gains on retained benchmarks.

T1.justification: Equations 1–26, including deformation, visibility, Gaussian rendering and loss definitions, remain mathematically unchanged. Appendix L adds an explanatory illustration of existing reasoning, without introducing a new formal assumption, derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: real-time photorealistic rendering through double unprojection, image-conditioned template deformation and Gaussian scale refinement. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 replaces the earlier loose-clothing and motion-capture caveats with finger-rigidity and topology-change limitations. Appendices K and M further discuss lighting adaptation, color fluctuations attributed to illumination overfitting, and degraded clothing-removal results. This substantially revises applicability boundaries; the point-cloud supervision limitation remains.

D1.justification: The new studies specify the perturbed joint and angle levels, and identify sparse target-lighting views and separate frames used for fine-tuning. Existing implementation libraries, hardware, hyperparameters and project access information remain unchanged. The new lighting experiment does not specify its fine-tuning budget.

R1.justification: v2 removes the HOOD and NeuralClothSim references together with the cloth-simulation future-work suggestion. The main related-work discussion and positioning against prior human-capture and rendering methods remain unchanged; most citation-number differences are renumbering.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely preserved. Local revisions include the limitations paragraph, expanded appendix overview and explanatory discussion, new appendix subsections I–M, updated affiliations, and acknowledgements. There is no extensive rewriting or restructuring of the existing paper.

P2.justification: The appendix gains substantial visual presentations of error sensitivity, clothing and hair dynamics, lighting adaptation, texture-deformation relationships, and topology changes in Figures 12–16. Table 4 gains an FPS column, and retained appendix tables and Figure 11 are rearranged. Existing main figures and comparison-table structures are preserved.

improvement.justification: Figures 12–16 and the revised limitations provide better evidence about robustness and failure boundaries than v1's brief caveats. The benefit is limited by the selected qualitative examples and incomplete lighting fine-tuning details; the dress example does not establish general loose-clothing robustness. The main quantitative evidence and core contribution remain stable.
